Reverse mode: the discrete adjoint

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-reverse.Rmd
methods-reverse.Rmd

The reverse mode of cppODE() returns a gradient at a cost independent of the number of parameters, as the discrete adjoint of the computed trajectory; cvode() computes the continuous adjoint. Symbols follow the notation table. Used from R through derivMode = "reverse" of cppODE(), the arguments cotangent, keepStore, store and adjoint of solveODE(), and adjointControl() and releaseStore().

Gradient of one objective

Parameter estimation needs the gradient of one number \(L\), a likelihood or a residual sum of squares, in all \(M\) parameters \(\theta\). With forward sensitivities, one tangent per parameter, it costs about \(M\) solves; the reverse mode needs one forward solve and one backward sweep, whatever \(M\) [1], [2]. With the solver steps \(\theta \to x_1 \to \dots \to x_N\), the gradient is the product of the Jacobians, \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_N}\, \frac{\partial x_N}{\partial x_{N-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial x_2}{\partial x_1}\, \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial \theta} . \] The forward mode multiplies from the right, through the \(n_x \times M\) sensitivities. The reverse mode multiplies from the left, through rows of length \(n_x\), the adjoint \(\lambda\). The factors depend on the states, so the reverse mode solves forward, stores what the factors need, then walks back.

A reverse solve returns a contraction: for a cotangent \(w \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{obs}} \times n_x}\) on the observed trajectory, one sweep returns \[ \bar\theta_j = \sum_{o=1}^{n_{\mathrm{obs}}} \sum_{i=1}^{n_x} w_{oi} \, \frac{\partial x_i(t_o)}{\partial \theta_j}, \qquad j = 1,\dots,M, \tag{1} \] with \(\theta = (x_0, p)\), \(M = n_x + n_p\), and \(w_o \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}\) the row of \(w\) at \(t_o\). For \(w_{oi} = \partial L/\partial x_i(t_o)\) (for least squares, the weighted residual), \(\bar\theta = \nabla_\theta L\). Several cotangents, as columns of a three-dimensional array, take one sweep each.

Example: two Euler steps

For \(\dot x = -k x\), two explicit Euler steps of size \(h\) and \(L = x_2\), each step multiplies by \(a = 1 - hk\): \[ x_1 = a\,x_0, \qquad x_2 = a\,x_1, \qquad L = x_2 = a^2 x_0 . \] A step has the derivatives \(\partial x_{n+1}/\partial k = -h\,x_n\) and \(\partial x_{n+1}/\partial x_n = a\).

Forward. The tangent \(s_n = \mathrm{d}x_n/\mathrm{d}k\) starts at \(s_0 = 0\): \[ s_1 = a\,s_0 - h\,x_0 = -h\,x_0, \qquad s_2 = a\,s_1 - h\,x_1 = -2h\,a\,x_0 . \] The derivative in \(x_0\) needs a second tangent, started at \(1\).

Reverse. The adjoint \(\lambda_n = \partial L/\partial x_n\) starts at \(\lambda_2 = 1\). Each transposed step passes \(a\lambda_{n+1}\) to the previous state and adds \(-h\,x_n\lambda_{n+1}\) to the parameter cotangent \(\bar k\): \[ \lambda_1 = a\,\lambda_2 = a, \qquad \bar k = -h\,x_1\lambda_2 = -h\,a\,x_0, \] \[ \lambda_0 = a\,\lambda_1 = a^2, \qquad \bar k = -h\,a\,x_0 - h\,x_0\lambda_1 = -2h\,a\,x_0 . \] One backward pass returns both derivatives and reads \(x_1\) and \(x_0\), which the forward run stores. A further parameter adds a tangent in the forward mode and one entry of \(\bar\theta\) in the reverse mode.

\(-2h(1-hk)\,x_0\) is the exact derivative of the computed \(L_h = (1-hk)^2 x_0\), not of the exact solution \(x(2h) = e^{-2hk}x_0\), whose derivative is \(-2h\,e^{-2hk}x_0\). At \(h = 0.5\), \(k = 1\), \(x_0 = 1\): \(L_h = 0.25\) with derivative \(-0.5\), exact value \(0.368\) with derivative \(-0.368\) (Discrete and continuous adjoints).

Adjoint equation

The time-continuous form evaluates (1) without the sensitivity \(S_p\) of Forward (1). The adjoint \(\lambda(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}\) runs backwards from the end of the observed interval, \[ \dot\lambda = -J(x, p, t)^{\mathsf T}\lambda, \qquad \lambda(T^+) = 0, \qquad \lambda(t_o^-) = \lambda(t_o^+) + w_o, \tag{2} \] the counterpart of \(\lambda_n = a\,\lambda_{n+1}\). Along the solution the Jacobian terms cancel, \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left(\lambda^{\mathsf T} S_p\right) = -\lambda^{\mathsf T} J S_p + \lambda^{\mathsf T}\! \left(J S_p + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right) = \lambda^{\mathsf T} \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}, \tag{3} \] so \(\lambda\) does not depend on the choice of \(\theta\). Integrating (3) over \([t_0, T]\), with the jumps giving the terms of (1), \[ \bar\theta = \left(\frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\! \lambda(t_0) + \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\! \int_{t_0}^{T} \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\, \mathrm{d}t . \tag{4} \] For \(\theta = (x_0, p)\) the outer factors are identities, and a reverse solve reports \[ \bar x_0 = \lambda(t_0), \qquad \bar p = \int_{t_0}^{T} \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\, \mathrm{d}t, \tag{5} \] the counterparts of \(\lambda_0\) and \(\bar k\), stacked in the row order of the tangent argument, states first. A reparametrization \((x_0, p) = \Phi(\theta)\) enters afterwards through the outer factors of (4), the chain rule of Forward (2) applied on the left. The cost is one backward solve of dimension \(n_x\) and a quadrature of dimension \(n_p\), whatever \(M\); \(\partial f/\partial p\) enters only contracted with \(\lambda\).

Discrete adjoint in cppODE()

cppODE(..., derivMode = "reverse") does not integrate (2). As in the Euler example, the forward run stores one checkpoint per accepted step. The backward sweep applies the transposed accepted steps, last to first, and accumulates the parameter part of (5). Step sizes are constants of the differentiated map (Internal numerical differentiation).

Adjoint of the step map

An adjoint sums over all later uses of a quantity, so unlike a dual number it is not computed alongside the value. cppDE keeps no tape: the step map is one accepted step of a known method on a fixed grid, and the transpose is written in closed form. A multistep step consists of the Nordsieck rescale and Pascal shift, the corrector, and the controller tail: \[ z^{\text{pred}} = A\, z^{\text{in}}, \tag{6} \] \[ \Delta^{(0)} = 0, \qquad \Delta^{(m+1)} = \Delta^{(m)} + s\, W^{-1} r\bigl(\Delta^{(m)}, z^{\text{pred}}, \theta\bigr), \quad m = 0, \dots, k-1, \tag{7} \] \[ z^{\text{out}} = B\, z^{\text{pred}} + c\, \Delta, \qquad \Delta = \Delta^{(k)}, \tag{8} \] with \(z\) the Nordsieck array, \(\Delta\) the correction, residual \(r(\Delta, z, \theta) = f(z_0 + \Delta, t_{n+1}, \theta) - (\ell z_1 + \Delta)/\gamma\) with step coefficients \(\gamma = h_n\beta_0\) and \(\ell\), iteration matrix \(W\) and scale \(s\) of Stepping (3)-(4), \(k\) iterations, and corrected state \(y = z_0^{\text{pred}} + \Delta\). \(A\), \(B\) and \(c\) act on the slot index only, equally for every state component, with coefficients from the Nordsieck carry (order, step-size history and counters). They are read off the stepper: a probe whose states are the Nordsieck slots, seeded with the identity in the \([\text{slot} \times \text{component}]\) array, runs through the forward-step routines and returns every column in one pass, so the adjoint uses exactly the forward coefficients.

The corrector is differentiated as the \(k\) forward iterations (7), with \(W\), the step size, the order and \(k\) held fixed. From the cotangent \(\bar\Delta^{(k)}\), each backward iteration takes one transposed solve and one product with \(J^{\mathsf T}\) at \(y^{(m)} = z_0^{\text{pred}} + \Delta^{(m)}\): \[ \mu_m = s\, W^{-\mathsf T} \bar\Delta^{(m+1)}, \qquad \bar\Delta^{(m)} = \bar\Delta^{(m+1)} + J(y^{(m)})^{\mathsf T}\mu_m - \mu_m/\gamma, \] and \(J(y^{(m)})^{\mathsf T}\mu_m\), \(-(\ell/\gamma)\,\mu_m\) and \((\partial f/\partial\theta)(y^{(m)})^{\mathsf T}\mu_m\) pass to \(z_0^{\text{pred}}\), \(z_1^{\text{pred}}\) and \(\theta\). The forward sensitivities take the same iterations on dual numbers (Forward sensitivities), so both differentiate the same map. Closing the corrector by the implicit function theorem instead differentiates an equation the solver never solved exactly; on a stiff model under adams that equation can be unstable at the chosen step sizes while the iterations taken are not, and the gradient diverges. A Rosenbrock step transposes to a stage recursion of six solves against one factorization, an explicit step to the backward recursion over the tableau.

The code generator emits \(J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\) and \((\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda\) beside the right-hand side. For a Rosenbrock method it also emits both applied to \(J v\), a second derivative, since the stages solve against a matrix built from the Jacobian.

Checkpoints and memory

A checkpoint holds the step-start state, the Nordsieck carry, time, step size, the controller operations applied to the Nordsieck carry afterwards and, for a multistep method, the corrector iterates. Memory is linear in the number of steps and holds no derivatives. Each iteration matrix is recorded once, as the point, time and \(\gamma_p\) of the factorization, and refactorized in the sweep once per run of steps that used it. Slot operators are cached by Nordsieck carry and step size, so the probe runs only where the controller changed the control state.

An observation at an interpolated time goes through the continuous extension of the step containing it. After the tail the probe holds a valid interpolant, whose value at the observation time is the row \(\partial x_{\text{interp}} / \partial (z^{\text{pred}}, \Delta)\).

Reuse of checkpoints

The sweep reads only the checkpoints, so value run and sweep can be separate calls, as a gradient needs the values to form the cotangent.

  • keepStore = TRUE without a cotangent runs the values and returns the checkpoints as $store.
  • store passes them to a later solve at the same times and parameters, which goes directly to the sweep; a store from other parameter values is rejected.
  • A three-dimensional cotangent sweeps one store per column: \(n_{\text{seed}}\) sweeps, one integration.
  • The checkpoints live until the garbage collector frees the store or releaseStore() frees them; a released store makes the solve integrate again.
  • derivMode = "forward-reverse" refuses both arguments, since checkpoints of that mode hold tangents that do not outlive the recording solve.

The reverse mode supports all four methods, time- and root-triggered events (Events in reverse mode), forcings, the batch entry point and the sparse linear solver. The code is in cppde_adjoint_step.hpp, cppde_reverse_step.hpp and cppde_reverse_trajectory.hpp.

Discrete and continuous adjoints

The discrete adjoint of cppODE() discretizes, then differentiates: it is the derivative of the steps the forward solver took. The continuous adjoint of cvode(), the adjoint sensitivity analysis (ASA) of CVODES, differentiates, then discretizes: a second integrator with separate step-size control solves (2) and (5) backwards over forward states interpolated between checkpoints [3] (cvode() and the CVODES adjoint).

With \(L\) the objective of the exact solution and \(L_h\) the value the solver returns, the discrete adjoint is \(\nabla_\theta L_h\) on the value-run grid, with corrector iterations and matrices as taken. For every method it equals the forward sensitivities on the same grid (sensErrCon = FALSE) up to rounding. The continuous adjoint approximates \(\nabla_\theta L\) to the discretization error of both solves, \(O(\mathrm{tol})\) away from \(\nabla_\theta L_h\); in the Euler example it would approximate \(-0.368\), not \(-0.5\).

The two adjoints. Both converge to \(\nabla_\theta L\) as the tolerance is lowered.
discrete adjoint continuous adjoint
call cppODE(..., derivMode = "reverse") cvode(..., derivMode = "reverse")
order discretize, then differentiate differentiate, then discretize
backward pass transposed steps, forward grid second integrator for (2)
forward states checkpoint per step checkpoint every asaCheckpoints steps, interpolated
implicit step \(k\) transposed solves, forward iteration matrix stiff linear ODE under error control
event transposed jump arithmetic restart with transposed saltation
result \(\nabla_\theta L_h\), as forward on the same grid \(\nabla_\theta L\) to \(O(\mathrm{tol})\)
consistent with value up to rounding to \(O(\mathrm{tol})\)

Consistency with the value. Line searches, trust-region ratios and gradient stopping tests assume the gradient is the derivative of the value. Near the optimum \(\nabla_\theta L\) shrinks to the size of an \(O(\mathrm{tol})\) error, and an inconsistent gradient points where the computed value does not decrease: the trust-region ratio degrades, the line search fails, and a gradient tolerance below the error is never reached. The discrete adjoint is the gradient of the value the optimizer sees.

Refined sweep. adjointControl(refine = TRUE) holds the sweep to the tolerances and differentiates the flow, the solution map of the ODE, instead of the step map. Like the continuous adjoint, the result is closer to \(\nabla_\theta L\) and differs from \(\nabla_\theta L_h\) by the order of the discretization error. It pays off where the value grid is too coarse for the derivative, such as a trajectory at rest crossed in a few steps (Grid and refinement of the sweep). A refined solve also returns $correction, per seed column the first-order change of the seeded functional from the computed to the differentiated trajectory; value plus correction and the refined gradient belong to one function (Value correction of the refined sweep).

Example: Michaelis-Menten conversion

\(x\) converts into \(y\) by Michaelis-Menten kinetics, \(y\) degrades at first order and is observed at eleven time points, \(L = \sum_o \bigl(y(t_o) - d_o\bigr)^2\). The cotangent \(w_o\) holds \(2\bigl(y(t_o) - d_o\bigr)\) in the column of \(y\). The cppODE() models use bdf and rb4.

library(cppDE)
eqns  <- c(x = "-k1*x/(Km + x)", y = "k1*x/(Km + x) - k2*y")
parms <- c(x = 2, y = 0, k1 = 1, Km = 0.5, k2 = 0.3)
times <- 0:10
data  <- c(0, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 1.15, 1.05, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5)

methods <- c("bdf", "rb4")
fwd <- lapply(setNames(nm = methods), function(m)
  cppODE(eqns, method = m, modelname = paste0("mmFwd_", m), compile = FALSE))
rev <- lapply(setNames(nm = methods), function(m)
  cppODE(eqns, method = m, derivMode = "reverse",
         modelname = paste0("mmRev_", m), compile = FALSE))
do.call(compile, c(unname(c(fwd, rev)), list(output = "mmNative")))

hasCvode <- codegenAvailable("cvode")
if (hasCvode) {
  asa <- cvode(eqns, derivMode = "reverse", modelname = "mmAsa", compile = FALSE)
  compile(asa, output = "mmCvode")
}

The CVODES adjoint keeps no store, so the value run takes a zero cotangent.

cotangent <- function(y) {
  w <- matrix(0, length(times), 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("x", "y")))
  w[, "y"] <- 2 * (y - data)
  w
}
gradForward <- function(tol, method = "bdf", sensErrCon = FALSE) {
  out <- solveODE(fwd[[method]], times, parms, abstol = tol, reltol = tol,
                  sensErrCon = sensErrCon)
  2 * colSums((out$variable[, "y"] - data) * out$tangent[, "y", ])
}
gradReverse <- function(tol, method = "bdf", adjoint = NULL) {
  val <- solveODE(rev[[method]], times, parms, abstol = tol, reltol = tol,
                  keepStore = TRUE)
  solveODE(rev[[method]], times, parms, abstol = tol, reltol = tol,
           store = val$store, cotangent = cotangent(val$variable[, "y"]),
           adjoint = adjoint)$cotangent[, 1]
}
gradAsa <- function(tol) {
  if (!hasCvode) return(rep(NA_real_, length(parms)))
  val <- solveODE(asa, times, parms, abstol = tol, reltol = tol,
                  cotangent = cotangent(0 * data))
  solveODE(asa, times, parms, abstol = tol, reltol = tol,
           cotangent = cotangent(val$variable[, "y"]))$cotangent[, 1]
}

exact <- gradForward(1e-12, "rb4", sensErrCon = TRUE)
exact
#>          x          y         k1         Km         k2 
#> -1.4861036 -0.8366524  0.7868458 -0.5163659  9.5726795

A forward solve at reltol = 1e-12 stands in for \(\nabla_\theta L\). The tables give the largest difference over the five entries, relative to the largest entry.

gap <- function(a, b) max(abs(a - b)) / max(abs(b))
tols <- 10^-(4:10)
gapTable <- function(method) {
  t(sapply(tols, function(tol) {
    forward <- gradForward(tol, method)
    discrete <- gradReverse(tol, method)
    refined <- gradReverse(tol, method, adjointControl(refine = TRUE))
    c(reltol = tol,
      "discrete vs forward" = gap(discrete, forward),
      "discrete vs exact" = gap(discrete, exact),
      "refine vs forward" = gap(refined, forward),
      "refine vs exact" = gap(refined, exact),
      "continuous vs exact" = gap(gradAsa(tol), exact))
  }))
}

The discrete adjoint matches the forward sensitivities to rounding, both being \(\nabla_\theta L_h\). The refined sweep differs from them by the order of the tolerance, being the derivative of the value plus $correction.

Choice of derivative mode

need choice
full sensitivity matrix \(S\), as for Gauss-Newton; cost grows with \(M\) forward mode
one contraction per sweep, cost independent of \(M\), gradient for an optimizer discrete adjoint
SUNDIALS backend required continuous adjoint
value grid does not resolve the derivative refine = TRUE
second derivatives Second derivatives

The dMod2 article on trust-region optimization compares Gauss-Newton with forward derivatives against SR1 with reverse derivatives on a real objective.
